lesson.title: No-do-support Drills
lesson.subtitle: Fifteen questions built with one verb flip — no do, no auxiliary

hook.title: The Flip English Forgot
hook.content: English needs a whole extra verb to ask 'Do you know?'. German needs none: Weißt du? — one flip, subject and verb swap places, question complete. This is not German being fancy; it is the older machinery. Early Modern English still flipped freely — 'Knowest thou?', 'Sawest thou him?' — and only later bolted on do-support. Every German yes/no question is a statement run through a machine English used to own: verb to the front, everything else stays.

footnotes.title: The Rise of Do
footnotes.content: Do-support spread through English questions and negations between 1400 and 1700. 'I know it not' became 'I do not know it'; 'Knowest thou?' became 'Do you know?'. German never ran this upgrade — which is why its questions look archaic and are actually just ancient.

pattern.title: Flip Mechanics
pattern.content: Statement: Du weißt es. Question: Weißt du es? Statement: Du kannst kommen. Question: Kannst du kommen? Statement: Er ist da. Question: Ist er da? The rule has one clause: the CONJUGATED verb goes to position 1; everything else holds still. W-questions are the same machine with a W-word taking position 1 and the verb demoted to position 2: Wo ist der Kaffee? Wann kommst du? And with modals, the bracket never opens: Kannst du morgen kommen? — flip the modal, keep the bracket.
pattern.linguist_note: Intonation-only questions exist in German too — 'Du kommst morgen?' with rising pitch, exactly like English. The verb-first form is the neutral, unmarked way; the rising statement is the surprised way.

exercises.prompt: Flip it: 'Du weißt es' as a yes/no question:
exercises.meaning: Do you know it? (Knowest thou it?)
exercises.explanation: Verb to position 1, subject second: Weißt du es? The 'tust du' option is the do-support German never grew.

exercises.prompt: Match each statement with its flipped question. Then recall earlier vocabulary in the short phrases:
exercises.target_answer: Du kannst kommen, Er ist da, Du hast Zeit, Du kommst morgen, Warum kommen wir, Wohin gehen wir, Wir können das Tier kennen, Das Bier ist billig
exercises.meaning: Kannst du kommen?; Ist er da?; Hast du Zeit?; Kommst du morgen?; Why are we coming; Where are we going to; We can know the animal; The beer is cheap
exercises.explanation: One flip each: the conjugated verb steps in front of the subject, nothing else moves.
The -st riding in front: Weißt du? — German's Knowest thou?, alive and daily.

exercises.prompt: How does German build this question word-for-word?
exercises.explanation: German flips the conjugated verb to position 1 ('Kommst du...'), and the separable prefix 'mit' waits at the end of the clause (weißt du das?). [Ref: Tust du morgen kommen?]

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'Do you know where the coffee is?'
exercises.target_answer: Weißt du wo der Kaffee ist
exercises.meaning: Do you know where the coffee is?

vocab_hints.note: the embedded question keeps verb-final inside it — der Kaffee ist

exercises.explanation: Flip for the main question (Weißt du) — and the embedded wo-clause quietly parks its verb (ist) at the end.

summary.outcome: Build yes/no and W-questions with a single verb flip — zero do-support.

use_example.german: Weißt du, wo der Kaffee ist?
use_example.english: Do you know where the coffee is?

summary.takeaway: Verb to position 1 for yes/no questions, position 2 after W-words — the flip English retired and German kept.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: word order & the subordinate clauses — why weil and dass throw the verb to the very end, like Old English did.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from No-do-support Drills (Do you know where the coffee is):
twist.target_answer: Weißt du wo der Kaffee ist
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Weißt du wo der Kaffee ist" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of No-do-support Drills without relying on short-term echo.

können.context_translation: I can come / I am able to come.
können.etymology_derivation: Originally meant "to know/understand". Preserved in English "can", "cunning" (knowing how), "uncanny", and "beyond my ken" (beyond my knowledge).

wann.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hwan — the exact twin of English when. [wiktionary]

wo.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hwēr/*hwar — the exact twin of English where; English kept the h (wh-), German dropped it. [wiktionary]

husten.context_phrase: Ich trinke Tee gegen den Husten.
husten.context_translation: I am drinking tea for the cough.
husten.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *hwōstō; no English cognate listed — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

t-shirt.etymology_derivation: Borrowed directly from English t-shirt — an English loan in German. [wiktionary]

paprika.context_phrase: Ich nehme Paprika für den Salat.
paprika.context_translation: I am taking paprika for the salad.
paprika.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Hungarian paprika, from Serbo-Croatian, ultimately from Latin piper, meaning pepper; English paprika is a parallel borrowing. [wiktionary]

letzte.context_phrase: Der letzte Bus fährt um elf.
letzte.context_translation: The last bus leaves at eleven.
letzte.etymology_derivation: Historically the superlative of lat — the twin of late; the entry lists English latest and last as cognates. [wiktionary]

krawatte.context_phrase: Im Büro trägt er Hemd und Krawatte.
krawatte.context_translation: At the office he wears a shirt and tie.
krawatte.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French cravate, a doublet of Kroate (Croat) - named for Croatian mercenaries; English cravat is the same word. [wiktionary]

gerne.etymology_derivation: Variant of gern, from Proto-Germanic *gernaz 'eager, willing' — the same word as English yearn (Middle English yern, listed on the page); ich spiele gerne is literally I play yearningly. [wiktionary]

angebot.context_translation: The offer is only valid today.
angebot.etymology_derivation: From anbieten, to offer — the old noun Bot is the Germanic twin of English bid: an offer is an up-bid. [wiktionary]

unterschrift.context_phrase: Ich brauche deine Unterschrift auf dem Formular.
unterschrift.context_translation: I need your signature on the form.
unterschrift.etymology_derivation: unter + Schrift (from unterschreiben) — literally underwrit, the Germanic calque of Latin subscriptio; schreiben is the Latin-loan twin of scribe. [wiktionary]
